To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the global concentration of N-acetylaspartate, the most abundant brain metabolite and a marker for neural integrity, is significantly decreased in patients with benign multiple sclerosis (MS), even in the absence of focal brain damage as detected by conventional MR imaging.
the NAA loss rate is similar for all MS subtypes and is not a predictor of benign MS.
patients with benign RR MS exhibit a 35% lower global concentration of NAA than controls and that the loss rates are comparable with those of other MS patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel, noninvasive technique for measuring NAA in the brain.
the neuro-axonal damage in patients with MS and its relationship to the clinical disease course.
the question of whether there is a relationship between the severity of the disease and the severity of the neurodegeneration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WBNAA is a sensitive and specific biomarker of neuro-axonal damage and is not an indicator of the benign disease course.
benign MS is not a disease of benign neural dysfunction.
benign MS patients do not have normal brain NAA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NAA loss in benign patients is similar to that in other patients, and the benign course is a consequence of the NAA loss being distributed to less important areas of the brain.
NAA is a sensitive marker for axonal damage in MS, and that the damage occurs early and is progressive.
the NAA marker is not a good predictor of the benign MS phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
benign MS should not be considered a benign condition.
benign MS is a clinical misnomer.
the benign RRMS course is not associated with minimal neural dysfunction as measured by WBNAA.
